Baby & Child

When worries keep a child from joining in

Updated: November 17, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Your child wants to learn to swim. On the way to lessons they ask again and again whether you will stay, and by the changing room their stomach hurts. Start with what is happening at the pool. Ask whether someone has frightened them, whether a task feels unsafe or whether the worry begins even before they reach the water.

Look at what worry is costing your child

Worry before something new is common. It becomes a reason to seek help when it keeps returning, feels hard to manage and gets in the way of sleep, school, friendships or activities the child wants to do. You do not need to wait a set number of months before asking for advice. Fear of separation, worry about being judged and worry across many situations can look different.

You might notice repeated requests for reassurance, tearfulness, irritability, tense muscles, a racing heart or a stomach ache. Some children avoid the feared situation so successfully that adults rarely see them distressed. Ask what they have begun to miss. Listen for a real safety issue, such as bullying or a frightening incident, and address that first.

What happens in an assessment

Bring an example from home and one from school or another setting. The clinician asks what the child fears, how often it happens, what they avoid and how their body feels. A questionnaire may help the conversation. There is no blood test that diagnoses an anxiety disorder. Physical symptoms sometimes need examination or tests for other causes. A clinician can also ask about low mood, sleep and, with a teenager, alcohol or other substances.

A panic attack is a sudden surge of intense fear or discomfort. A pounding heart, dizziness, shaking, rapid breathing or feeling that things are unreal may accompany it. A first unexplained episode needs medical assessment. Severe trouble breathing, blue or grey lips, collapse or failure to respond needs emergency help. Do not assume these are signs of anxiety.

Choose a small, supported step

Acknowledge the fear and ask what the child would like to do again. If the pool is safe and the instructor agrees, a first step might be visiting at a quiet time to watch a lesson together. Decide on a next step the child can practise with support. Avoid surprising or forcing a frightened child into the water. Regular sleep, meals and activity are useful background support; no particular food cures an anxiety disorder.

Cognitive behavioural therapy helps children recognise anxious predictions and practise approaching safe situations gradually. A clinician may consider medicine for some children and monitor its effects. In a trial of 488 young people aged 7 to 17 with separation anxiety, generalized anxiety or social anxiety, about 81% receiving cognitive behavioural therapy with sertraline and 60% receiving therapy alone were rated much or very much improved after 12 weeks. These outcomes are not a prescription for an individual child and do not apply to every form of anxiety.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Listen to the child’s explanation and investigate any real threat.

Ask a professional about persistent distress or avoidance affecting home or school.

Plan small achievable steps and review what helped.

How BeMama can help

BeMama suggests asking “What would you like to be able to do again?” and taking that example to the appointment. It gives the child a say in what support should help them achieve.

When to seek help

Get emergency help for severe breathing difficulty, blue or grey lips, collapse or an unresponsive child. A first unexplained panic-like episode needs medical assessment.

Evidence notes updated: November 17, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Notice what your child has stopped doing as well as what they say they fear.
  • Ask for assessment when anxiety limits ordinary life, and have new physical symptoms assessed.
  • Agree on a small, safe step with the child and their care team.

Frequently asked questions

What is an anxiety disorder?

A pattern of fear or worry that is excessive for the situation, causes distress or disrupts daily life may be an anxiety disorder. The clinician considers the child’s age, context and the whole pattern.

What signs are common?

Children may repeatedly seek reassurance, avoid activities, become irritable or sleep poorly. Some have stomach aches, tense muscles or a racing heart. Ask where the symptoms occur and how they affect the child.

Is there a test for anxiety?

An interview with the child and caregiver and sometimes a questionnaire help the clinician assess the pattern. Tests may be needed to investigate physical symptoms, but no single laboratory test diagnoses anxiety.

What might a panic attack feel like?

Fear may surge suddenly with shaking, dizziness, a pounding heart, fast breathing or a sense that things are unreal. Ask for medical advice for a first unexplained episode. Severe breathing difficulty, collapse, blue lips or unresponsiveness are emergencies.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
